openers.resilience-thresholds-and-limits: Every environment has a ceiling: the largest population of a species it can keep going on its food, water and habitat. This chapter is about what happens near such limits. When conditions change sharply, many ecosystems resist the damage and recover. Yet a fairly small change in outside conditions can sometimes set off a rapid change, and a system's state can depend on its history as much as on the present. Making sense of this means looking at wholes and at loops of cause and effect, and the same questions reach people: how many of us can the Earth support?

nature-eco-593.title: Carrying capacity: how many any place can feed
nature-eco-593.text: Any patch of land or water can feed only so many mouths. Ecologists call that ceiling the carrying capacity: the largest population of a species an environment can keep going over time, given its food, habitat, water and other resources. Below carrying capacity, a {{ref:nature-eco-374}} can grow, as {{ref:nature-eco-376}} describes. Above it, numbers usually shrink for lack of space, food or sunlight. At the ceiling itself, births equal deaths once animals moving in and out are counted, so the population sits in equilibrium. Whatever stops growth is called the limiting factor. It might be food, water or nesting space, or even the amount of waste the environment can absorb. Applied to a whole environment, the idea means resources are not taken faster than they regrow, and wastes stay within what nature can absorb. The term spread through biology in the 1870s. Wildlife and livestock managers developed it in the early 1900s, and it was a staple of ecology by the 1950s. Today it is used to find the maximum population an environment can support in ecology, farming and fisheries. Many authors still doubt its value for wild populations, because it can oversimplify how species interact.

nature-eco-638.title: Feedback: when outputs loop back as inputs
nature-eco-638.text: In 270 BC an inventor in Alexandria built a float valve that kept water at a constant level. It is the first known artificial feedback device. Feedback is what happens when a system's outputs loop back to become its inputs, forming a circuit of cause and effect. Because each part influences the other, simple cause-and-effect reasoning fails, and the system must be analyzed as a whole. The idea entered economic theory in Britain by the 18th century, though it did not yet have a name. In nature the stakes are high. In organisms, ecosystems and the biosphere, most quantities must be held within a narrow range around an optimal level. The climate system has strong loops that amplify change and others that damp it, linking atmosphere, ocean and land; {{ref:nature-eco-639}} explains the two kinds. Many systems with several loops, though, cannot be classed simply as one kind or the other.

nature-eco-624.title: Fire, flood and fallen trees: how disturbance shapes ecosystems
nature-eco-624.text: A single tree crashing down counts. So does a mass extinction. Both are disturbances: changes in environmental conditions that cause a marked change in an {{ref:nature-found-015}}. The list includes fires, floods, storms, insect outbreaks, trampling, earthquakes, plant diseases and volcanic eruptions. Disturbance is not simply damage. Many ecosystems are kept going by it; wetlands, for example, by moving water and periodic fires. Right after a disturbance comes a pulse of regrowth, because competition for space and resources is low. Many shade-intolerant plants need such openings to establish, so biological diversity depends on natural disturbance. In western US ponderosa pine forests, suppressing surface fires lets dense Douglas fir take over, cutting light, plant diversity and the animals that rely on them. How species cope with disturbance may even predict how well they adapt to {{ref:nature-hist-007}}.

nature-eco-603.title: Ecological resilience: taking a blow and recovering
nature-eco-603.text: A forest can usually recover when lightning or landslides damage up to 10 percent of its area. Beyond that, recovery gets harder. This capacity to resist damage from a disturbance and then recover is called ecological resilience. Canadian ecologist C.S. Holling introduced the idea to describe how natural systems persist through change. The shocks can be natural, such as fires, floods, windstorms and insect outbreaks. They can also be human: deforestation, pesticide use and the introduction of exotic species. A large or long enough {{ref:nature-eco-624}} can push an ecosystem past a threshold into a different regime, a new set of processes and structures. Biodiversity loss, resource exploitation, pollution, changes in how land is used, and climate change increasingly cause such shifts, often to degraded states. The IPCC, the international panel that assesses climate science, widened the idea in its Sixth Assessment Report. Besides keeping function, identity and structure, resilience there includes the capacity to transform. The lesson for managers is practical. Using nature's goods and services sustainably requires understanding an ecosystem's resilience and its limits. Interest has shifted away from {{ref:nature-res-013}} toward managing whole ecosystems to build resilience, with management and governance that learn and adjust.

nature-eco-628.title: Ecological stability: one word, 167 definitions
nature-eco-628.text: In 1997 Grimm and Wissel counted the meanings of stability in the ecological literature. They found 167 definitions covering 70 different concepts. Broadly, ecological stability is an ecosystem's ability to return to equilibrium after a {{ref:nature-eco-624}}, or to avoid sudden large changes over time. The catch is that an ecosystem can be stable in some properties and not others. A plant community in drought may keep its biomass while losing biodiversity. Some ecosystems are not stable at all, as with the wolves and moose of Isle Royale. The concept emerged in the first half of the 20th century and spread with theoretical ecology in the 1970s. Overuse of the term has made its definition a matter of controversy. Grimm and Wissel proposed replacing it with more specific terms such as constancy, resilience and persistence.

nature-eco-635.title: Ecosystem health: a useful metaphor or a value judgment?
nature-eco-635.text: {{ref:nature-hist-051}} wrote of land health and land sickness, and the metaphor goes back at least to the early 1800s. Ecosystem health is that metaphor: a way of describing the overall condition of an {{ref:nature-found-015}}. Fire, drought, invasive species, climate change, mining, fishing, farming and logging can all change that condition. The Great Lakes Basin tracks it with a suite of 80 lake health indicators, including native fish, phosphorus and toxic chemicals. Yet there is no universal benchmark. Judgments depend on the measures chosen and on society's goals. Species in an ecosystem also reshuffle over time, so a healthy state is hard to pin down. Supporters value the idea as a simple way to communicate. Critics argue it is a value judgment passed off as science, and propose neutral terms such as ecosystem status, ecosystem prognosis or ecosystem sustainability.

nature-eco-642.title: Overshoot: growing past the limit, then crashing
nature-eco-642.text: In 1944, 29 reindeer were introduced to St. Matthew Island. By 1963 there were about 6000. By 1965 there were 42. That boom and bust is overshoot: a population growing beyond its local {{ref:nature-eco-593}}, using resources faster than they can be replaced. When resources are depleted faster than they regenerate, a crash can follow, a path called overshoot-and-collapse. Overshoot can happen because impacts are delayed, so births keep exceeding deaths. People are not exempt. In the Horn of Africa, after smallpox was eradicated, a herding population of about 1 million grew to 14 million, causing overgrazing and soil erosion. Prolonged overshoot can profoundly change and simplify entire ecosystems.

nature-eco-640.title: Hysteresis: when a system remembers its past
nature-eco-640.text: A thermostat that turns the heat on below 18 °C but off only above 22 °C uses hysteresis on purpose. Sir James Alfred Ewing coined the word in 1881, from a Greek term meaning 'lagging behind'. It describes a system whose state depends on its history, not just on present conditions. Agar melts at 85 °C but solidifies only at 32 to 40 °C. Between those temperatures, whether it is liquid or solid depends on where it started. Plotted on a graph, such systems often trace a hysteresis loop: one variable takes different values depending on which way another variable is changing. In ecology, this means environmental conditions alone cannot predict a system's equilibrium. Its past matters too, as spruce budworm outbreaks show.

nature-eco-596.title: How many people can the Earth support?
nature-eco-596.text: In 10,000 BCE between 5 and 10 million people lived on Earth. By 1900 there were 1.5 billion. The agricultural and industrial revolutions had raised human carrying capacity. This is the number of people the Earth or a region can support, and it depends on how people live and the technology they use. Without the Haber-Bosch process for fixing nitrogen, described in {{ref:nature-eco-230}}, modern agriculture could not support 8 billion people. These successes have come at grave cost, from climate change and ocean acidification to dead zones at river mouths. Degrading the ecosystem services people depend on could lower the ceiling again. Measuring it is arbitrary, because what counts as food or water, and trade between regions, change the answer. A 2004 review of 69 studies found an average predicted maximum of 7.7 billion, with bounds of 0.65 and 98 billion. Some argue 8 billion may already be too many. Sources disagree on that, and on how far technology can raise the limit.

nature-eco-594.title: The logistic equation: growth that levels off at K
nature-eco-594.text: In 1838 Pierre François Verhulst published equations for how populations level off, without ever using the term carrying capacity. Written today, his equation reads dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K). Here dN/dt is the rate at which the population changes, N is population size, r is the intrinsic rate of natural increase and K is the {{ref:nature-eco-593}}. The letter K comes from the German Kapazitätsgrenze, meaning capacity limit. The logic sits in the bracket. When the population is small, the bracket is close to one and numbers grow exponentially. As N nears K, the bracket shrinks toward zero, and so does growth. Solving the equation gives the S-shaped logistic growth curve N(t) = K/(1 + Ae^(−rt)), the pattern traced in {{ref:nature-eco-376}}.

nature-eco-652.title: Systems thinking: seeing wholes instead of parts
nature-eco-652.text: {{ref:nature-hist-059}} described leverage points: places in a system where a small change can produce a large shift in behavior. Her idea belongs to systems thinking, a way of understanding complexity by looking at wholes and the relationships between parts rather than breaking things into pieces. A system here is a set of interconnected things that produce their own pattern of behavior over time. Ludwig von Bertalanffy and Jay Forrester were early contributors, and Peter Senge's The Fifth Discipline popularized the approach in the 1990s. Its methods include {{ref:nature-es-077}}, which models {{ref:nature-econ-595}} together with internal feedback loops. The goal is practical: finding effective action in complex situations and bringing about systems change. {{ref:nature-eecon-059}}, for instance, criticizes the concept of an {{ref:nature-found-031}} for lacking systems thinking.

nature-eco-592.title: Ecological thresholds: the small push that flips a system
nature-eco-592.text: Clear lakes turning murky is a well documented example. A database kept by the Resilience Alliance and the Santa Fe Institute lists over one hundred cases like it. Each involves an ecological threshold: the point at which a fairly small change in outside conditions sets off a rapid change in an ecosystem. Thresholds show that ecosystems respond non-linearly, so pressure does not produce proportional change. Some are sharp points; others are zones where the shift is gradual. Once one is passed, the ecosystem's own {{ref:nature-eco-603}} may not bring it back. Many crossed thresholds have proved hard or nearly impossible to undo, earning the name points of no return; extinction is the definitive example. The way back often differs from the way there, a property called {{ref:nature-eco-640}}. Thresholds are not always easy to detect. One approach scans time series, long runs of measurements, for a sudden jump. Close relatives include critical load, critical transition, {{ref:nature-eco-613}} and {{ref:nature-eco-607}}.

nature-eco-597.title: Planetary boundaries: nine limits for a livable Earth
nature-eco-597.text: In 2009 scientists led by Johan Rockström of the Stockholm Resilience Centre and Will Steffen of the Australian National University set out limits for the whole planet. Planetary boundaries mark how far human activity can push the Earth system before it may stop regulating itself. Crossing them could push the Earth out of the Holocene, the stable period in which human society developed. Worse, the authors warned, transgressing a boundary risks crossing thresholds that trigger abrupt, non-linear change at continental to planetary scale, the behavior described in {{ref:nature-eco-592}}. There are nine boundaries. They cover climate change, ocean acidification, loss of stratospheric ozone, nitrogen and phosphorus flows, freshwater use, land system change, biosphere integrity, chemical pollution and atmospheric aerosol loading. The count of breaches keeps rising. Three were judged crossed in 2009 and four in the 2015 update. Novel entities, meaning new human-made substances, became the fifth in 2022, freshwater change the sixth in 2023 and ocean acidification the seventh in 2025. Agriculture and food help push four of the nine past their limits, with surplus nitrogen and phosphorus flows the most important. Politics followed the science. UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon endorsed the concept in 2012. It was later dropped from the text of {{ref:nature-hist-008}}, because poorer countries worried it would sideline development.

nature-eco-607.title: Climate tipping points: thresholds with no easy way back
nature-eco-607.text: Early IPCC work judged climate tipping likely only above 4 °C of warming. By 2021 it was considered significantly probable at just over 1 °C, and highly probable above 2 °C. A tipping point is the climate's version of an {{ref:nature-eco-592}}: a critical threshold that, once crossed, leads to large, accelerating and often irreversible change. The IPCC defines it as a threshold beyond which a system reorganizes, often abruptly or irreversibly. A small disturbance can cause a disproportionately large change, often through self-reinforcing {{ref:nature-eco-638}}. Tipping behavior appears in ice sheets, glaciers, ocean circulation, ecosystems and the atmosphere. Thawing permafrost, ground that stays frozen, can release methane. Melting ice makes Earth less reflective. Both would speed warming. Crossing tipping points would likely have severe impacts on human society and could accelerate global warming.

nature-eco-632.title: Ecosystem collapse: when a living system loses itself
nature-eco-632.text: Consider the reefs described in {{ref:nature-eco-453}}. Even at 1.5 °C of warming, only 0.2% of the world's reefs could withstand marine heatwaves, against 84% now. Losses like that are what ecologists mean by ecosystem collapse. An ecosystem loses its defining features, and the ecosystem services it provided, once destabilizing pressures push it past a critical threshold. Collapse does not mean all life disappears. The original ecosystem is replaced by a novel one with greatly altered structure and function. Some have called it the ecosystem version of species extinction. It is usually irreversible, and any recovery is slow and needs active intervention. Human drivers include introduced species, overexploitation, pollution, climate change and habitat destruction or fragmentation. Collapse can also occur when an ecosystem shrinks below a minimum viable size or loses key biological processes. The timeline may be short. Under a high-emissions scenario, tropical ocean ecosystems could face abrupt disruption before 2030, with forests in the tropics and polar regions following by 2050. Little is known yet about effective ways to conserve or reverse collapsing ecosystems.

nature-eco-613.title: Regime shifts: abrupt, lasting changes in how systems work
nature-eco-613.text: In the 1990s strong evidence arrived from four kinds of places: {{ref:nature-eco-422}}, {{ref:nature-eco-453}}, {{ref:nature-eco-520}} and shallow lakes. All showed regime shifts, large, abrupt and lasting changes in how a complex system is structured and works. The system can be an ecosystem, the climate or a financial system. A regime is its typical behavior, held in place by loops of {{ref:nature-eco-638}} that reinforce one another. Shifts happen when those stabilizing loops weaken, or when an outside shock exceeds what the system can absorb. A small disturbance can produce big effects, so inputs and outputs are not proportional. In ecology, shifts can sharply change flows of food, clean water and {{ref:nature-es-121}}. They are hard to reverse and sometimes irreversible. Deforestation could shift Amazon and East Asian rainforests toward savanna, affecting food, fresh water, the climate and biodiversity. Shifts are expected to grow more common as human influence on the planet grows. Yet there is no agreed definition, and how to apply the concept remains contested.

nature-eco-598.title: Measuring the boundaries: from 280 to 423 parts per million
nature-eco-598.text: The climate boundary sits at 350 parts per million (ppm) of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. Before industry the level was 280 ppm; today it is 423 ppm. That trio of numbers shows how the {{ref:nature-eco-597}} framework works. Each boundary has a control variable, a measurable quantity with a limit value, used to track how far humanity has shifted the Earth away from Holocene conditions. The 2009 study quantified seven of the nine boundaries; by 2025 eight were quantified. The gaps can be wide. Biosphere integrity has a limit of under 10 extinctions per million species-years, where a species-year is one species existing for one year. The current rate is over 100. The land system boundary keeps 75% of forests intact, while the global figure is 59%. Industrial and intentional nitrogen fixation has a limit of 62 teragrams (million tonnes) per year, against a current 165. Only two boundaries, aerosol loading and loss of stratospheric ozone, are listed as not exceeded. For several processes no single threshold point can be located, because the Earth system is complex and evidence is still partial.

nature-eco-604.title: Bouncing back versus holding on: two kinds of resilience
nature-eco-604.text: Some shallow lakes can exist in two quite different forms. In one, the water is clear and rich in ecosystem services. In the other, it is turbid, poorer in services and prone to toxic algae blooms. Which one a lake sits in depends on phosphorus. Resilience, introduced in {{ref:nature-eco-603}}, has two distinct meanings. The first is how fast a system returns to equilibrium after a shock. C.S. Holling called this engineering resilience, because physics and engineering use it. The second, ecological resilience, is how much disturbance a system can absorb while keeping the same function and structure. It assumes a system can exist in several stable states, or regimes, like those lakes. Australia's Mulga woodlands are another case. Fire, grazing animals and rainfall can leave them grass-rich and good for sheep, or shrub-dominated and useless for grazing.

nature-eco-616.title: Alternative stable states: one place, two possible ecosystems
nature-eco-616.text: A reef can flip from coral-dominated to a degraded, algae-dominated system when the animals that graze on algae decline. Richard Lewontin first proposed the theory of alternative stable states in 1969. It holds that an ecosystem can settle into more than one stable state under the same conditions. A move between them, called a state shift, phase shift or regime shift, happens when the ecosystem is perturbed. Feedbacks make each state resist shifting, so the system stays put unless the push is large enough. The states are separated by ecological thresholds, unlike ecosystems that change smoothly along a gradient. The evidence is mixed. A 2005 review found 21 valid direct experiments, of which 14 supported the theory and 8 did not. If such states exist, gradual change may have little effect until a threshold triggers a catastrophic shift, which matters for monitoring and restoration.

nature-eco-653.title: Human ecology: people inside their environments
nature-eco-653.text: A city leans on far more land than lies inside its limits: typically at least ten times as much. Human ecology studies ties like these, the ways humans relate to their natural, social and built environments. It emerged from ecology and the social sciences in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It examines how populations adapt to environments and how technology and economies shape sustainability, extending the study of {{ref:nature-eco-129}}.

nature-eco-608.title: Ice sheets, currents and forests: the climate's tipping elements
nature-eco-608.text: Completely melting the Greenland ice sheet would raise global sea levels by 7.2 metres. That ice sheet is one of the climate's tipping elements: parts of the climate system, such as ice sheets, ocean currents and large forests, that may have {{ref:nature-eco-607}}. As of September 2022, researchers had identified nine global core tipping elements and seven regional impact tipping elements. Several are likely to tip at 1.5 °C of warming. They include the collapse of the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets, the die-off of tropical reef corals and abrupt thaw of northern permafrost. The stakes are large. Around 500 million people depend on reefs, and a sustained ocean temperature rise of 1 °C above average is enough to cause bleaching, the whitening of stressed coral. The Atlantic overturning circulation is a vast system of ocean currents. Its collapse would cool parts of Europe by over 10 °C and threaten crop yields across most world regions. Permafrost holds carbon from organisms that died over thousands of years.

nature-eco-639.title: Positive and negative feedback: amplify or correct
nature-eco-639.text: When snow melts, it exposes darker ground. The dark ground absorbs more heat, which melts more snow. That loop is positive feedback, which amplifies a change. Here positive means reinforcing, not good. Negative, or balancing, feedback does the opposite and counteracts a change. Put precisely, positive feedback widens the gap between a target and the actual value, and negative feedback narrows it. Both are kinds of {{ref:nature-eco-638}}, and they also go by the names self-reinforcing and self-correcting. A car's cruise control, which holds a target speed, is negative feedback at work. Negative feedback is often added deliberately to make a system more stable and accurate.
